The LGCC meetings will be conducted in a hybrid format allowing the public to participate 
either in person or remotely. 
 
Viewing: The public will have the ability to view meetings by attending in-person or 
by tuning into the APS Board of Education YouTube Channel.  
 
Public Comment Sign Up and Submission Instructions: 
▪ Written Public Comments: The LGCC will take public comments in written 
form by submitting comments to boarded@aps.edu. Written comments will be 
distributed to all LGCC members for review. 
▪ Virtual, Live Public Comment: The LGCC will hear general public comments 
on a first-come, first-serve basis. To provide live public comment over Zoom, 
participants must sign up for public comment at using the APS Public 
Comment Committee Form by 3:30 p.m. the day of the LGCC meeting. 
 
Note: If providing public comments via Zoom, speakers must enter the Zoom 
meeting with the name used to sign-up to speak so speakers can be identified and 
access the meeting remotely. A Zoom link will be e-mailed to remote participants 
immediately following completion of the comment form. 
Public Comment Rules: Each participant has two minutes to speak. Comments are 
to be addressed to the LGCC members only, through the Chair. Any disruptive 
conduct will result in removal from the meeting. 
Remote participants will be an "Attendee" in the Zoom meeting until the public 
comment period begins. The moderator will move the speaker into the live meeting 
as a "Panelist" when prompted to provide comments. 
 
 
 
NOTICE TO PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES: 
If you are an individual with a disability who is in need of a reader, amplifier, qualified sign 
language interpreter or any form of auxiliary aid or service to attend or participate in the 
hearing(s) or meeting(s), please contact the Commission Administrator at (505) 468-7083 or 
TDD (505) 468-7088 at least one week prior to the meeting or as soon as possible. Public 
documents, including the agenda and minutes, can be provided in various accessible formats. 
Please contact the County Manager’s Office at either of the above numbers if a summary or 
other type of accessible format is needed.

records.text: Local Government Coordinating Commission Information about the Local Government Coordinating Commission (LGCC). https://www.cabq.gov/council/albuquerque-bernalillo-county-government-commission https://www.cabq.gov/++resource++plone-logo.svg Local Government Coordinating Commission Information about the Local Government Coordinating Commission (LGCC). https://www.cabq.gov/council/albuquerque-bernalillo-county-government-commission https://www.cabq.gov/++resource++plone-logo.svg Local Government Coordinating Commission Information about the Local Government Coordinating Commission (LGCC). About LGCC Formerly known as Albuquerque Bernalillo County Government Commission (ABCGC), the Local Government Coordinating Commission is a joint City of Albuquerque, Bernalillo County, and Albuquerque Public Schools Commission made up of elected officials for the purpose of discussing topics of common interest, long-range goals, community needs and other items as requested by the respective bodies. The LGCC makes recommendations to those bodies. The Council President appoints the 4 Council members, subject to approval of the Council; the Mayor also sits on this committee. The Chair of the Board of County Commissioners appoints the 4 County Commission members. The President of the APS Board of Education appoints the 2 Board members. The Chair of the LGCC alternates each year beginning in January, between the City, County, and APS District. The LGCC meets on a regular basis. The LGCC meetings will be conducted in a hybrid format allowing the public to participate 
either in person or remotely. 
 
Viewing: The public will have the ability to view meetings by attending in-person or 
by tuning into the APS Board of Education YouTube Channel.  
 
Public Comment Sign Up and Submission Instructions: 
▪ Written Public Comments: The LGCC will take public comments in written 
form by submitting comments to boarded@aps.edu. Written comments will be 
distributed to all LGCC members for review. 
▪ Virtual, Live Public Comment: The LGCC will hear general public comments 
on a first-come, first-serve basis. To provide live public comment over Zoom, 
participants must sign up for public comment at using the APS Public 
Comment Committee Form by 3:30 p.m. the day of the LGCC meeting. 
 
Note: If providing public comments via Zoom, speakers must enter the Zoom 
meeting with the name used to sign-up to speak so speakers can be identified and 
access the meeting remotely. A Zoom link will be e-mailed to remote participants 
immediately following completion of the comment form. 
Public Comment Rules: Each participant has two minutes to speak. Comments are 
to be addressed to the LGCC members only, through the Chair. Any disruptive 
conduct will result in removal from the meeting. 
Remote participants will be an "Attendee" in the Zoom meeting until the public 
comment period begins. The moderator will move the speaker into the live meeting 
as a "Panelist" when prompted to provide comments.

PROGRAM OVERVIEW 
Accountable Entity: 1) Identify the designated accountable entity responsible for fiscal, 
administrative, and operational oversight of the regional plan. Describe the accountable entity’s 
roles and responsibilities, including governance, decision-making authority, and coordination 
with regional partners. 2) Explain how the accountable entity will ensure accountability, 
compliance, and effective implementation of the regional plan 
On June 28th, 2024, the BernCo Board of Commissioners enacted a Behavioral Health Ordinance 
that mandated the creation of a Behavioral Health Authority Division (BHAD), led by a new 
Deputy County Manager (DCM). The Ordinance also sets the expectation that BHAD would issue 
three year strategic plans and establish three new advisory bodies.  
BHAD is close to completing the implementation of the first year of its BH Strategic Plan focused 
over the next three years on building the capacity and infrastructure required to assure that 
BernCo further builds and sustains a comprehensive BH continuum of care. During this process 
BHAD has established two new departments, one entitled Operational Supports and the other, 
Integrated Services. Within these departments are functional entities that focus on prevention, 
intervention, crisis response, treatment recovery supports, quality management, data 
collection, analysis, and reporting, and resource development. These capabilities have 
positioned BernCo to serve as the Accountable Entity under the Behavioral Health Reform and 
Investment Act (BHRIA) for Region 2.  
When the BHRIA was signed into law, by the Governor, on February 27, 2025, Bernalillo County 
(BernCo) was already in alignment with its goals. BernCo has partnered with the City of 
Albuquerque (CABQ) in this role. As part of the Mini Grant Application, through the 
Administrative Offices of the Courts (AOC), the CABQ and the Pueblo of Isleta each provided 
letters of support for BernCo to serve as the Accountable Entity. Later, both governments 
executed Memorandum of Understandings (MOUs) with the Accountable Entity.  
Subsequently, BernCo hosted the Enhanced Sequential Intercept Model (ESIM) event, five 
listening sessions, with one dedicated specifically to tribal collaboration. In addition, BernCo has 
had leadership representation at all of the BHRIA Executive Committee meetings, has 
participated in the Technical Assistance offered through the University of New Mexico ECHO 
program, and has comprised and convened a Stakeholder Committee in accordance with the  
BHRIA statute.  
While BernCo is serving in a leadership role for Region 2, BHRIA emphasizes a community-
centered and stakeholder-driven process to strengthen the behavioral health (BH) continuum  

 
 
 
 
6 
 
of care. In response, Region 2’s Stakeholder Committee has guided the Regional Plan with the 
endorsement of the Albuquerque City Council, the Bernalillo County Board of Commissioners, 
the Criminal Justice Coordinating Council, and the Health Equity Council. This structure was 
designed to ensure that all community stakeholders have an opportunity to engage in 
establishing regional priorities. Further, the Stakeholder Committee meetings are open 
meetings and allow for public comment, again providing an opportunity for broad participation. 
Throughout the planning process, BernCo retained final decision-making authority to ensure 
timely implementation and alignment with statutory requirements and BHRIA deadlines.  
BernCo will utilize its data, quality, and contract management capabilities to manage all 
proposals funded under the BHRIA allocations to Region 2. In addition, BernCo intends to utilize 
one or more of the following vehicles to manage the process for expedited grant awards to 
services providers:  
1. Multi-awards to overgo provider organizations.  
2. Intergovernmental Agreements (IGA). 
3. The Health Care Authority’s (HCA) Administrative Services Organization (ASO). BernCo is 
already a contracted BH Service Provider under the ASO.   
The intent, regardless of the structure is to distribute funds to service providers, to develop a 
user-friendly data collection tool for monthly reporting that will then be utilized to provide 
quarterly reports as required by BHRIA. This monthly tracking and monitoring will enable 
BernCo to identify provider challenges early in the process and appropriately intervene.  
Governance and Accountability Structure 
Implementation of the Regional Plan is guided by a structured governance framework: 
 
Accountable Entity (BernCo/BHAD): Final authority for funding decisions, contract 
management, and compliance assurance. 
 
Stakeholder Committee: Advisory body responsible for the refinement of regional 
priorities and the integration of community input. 
 
Behavioral Health Advisory Board (BHAB): Oversight, policy alignment, and annual 
reporting review. 
 
Office of Quality Management (OQM): Performance monitoring, continuous quality 
improvement, and corrective action plan management. 
 
Office of Data Collection, Analysis, and Reporting (ODCAR): Data integration, analysis, 
and dashboard reporting.  
 
Escalation protocols will include technical assistance, Corrective Action Plans (CAPs), enhanced 
monitoring, and potential contract termination. 

 
 
 
 
7 
 
Stakeholder Engagement: 1) Describe how stakeholders are meaningfully engaged in the 
development, implementation, and ongoing oversight of the regional plan. 2) Identify 
participating groups, including counties, Tribes, Pueblos, Nations, service systems, and 
individuals with lived experience. 3) Describe outreach methods, coordination mechanisms, and 
structured processes for gathering input, collaboration, feedback, and continuous 
improvements of the regional plan.  
Region 2 consists of BernCo, CABQ, Isleta Pueblo, Sandia Pueblo, and To’Hajiilee Navajo Chapter. 
At the time of the submission of this Plan, Sandia has remained in deliberations regarding their 
participation in BHRIA-related regional planning. Concerns related to data sovereignty appeared 
to be a major outstanding issue. Recently, Region 2 was notified by the HCA that To’Hajiilee will 
not be incorporated into Region 2 planning, but will instead be included in BHRIA planning 
under the Navajo Nation. 
BernCo contracted with Bronwyn Neeser, PhD, as the Project Lead to facilitate BHRIA Regional 
Planning. During the initial phase of BHRIA, Dr. Neeser set up meetings with local providers, 
toured facilities, and presented at a number of community meetings regarding BHRIA and 
regional planning. Through these initial contacts, access to various listservs allowed information 
to be distributed to larger groups. These capabilities, along with BernCo’s Communication and 
Public Relation assets (including, a dedicated BernCo web portal for BHRIA content), have been 
utilized to make information available to community members. BernCo has taken “a no-wrong-
door” approach to BHRIA, meaning if anyone reaches out requesting a meeting, one is 
scheduled as soon as practicable.  
The Stakeholder Committee is made up of all the sector representatives outlined in statute. In 
addition, Law Enforcement, the Albuquerque Public Schools (APS), and representatives of the 
BernCo Behavioral Health Advisory Board (BHAB), are active members. Once the BHRIA 
Executive Committee has accepted the Region 2 Plan, BHAD will guide the implementation and 
ongoing operation of BHRIA projects. Presentations related to the progress of BHRIA planning 
have been given to the Local BH Health Collaborative, the Coalition for a Safer Albuquerque, the 
Addiction Treatment Advisory Board (ATAB), and the Community Care Collective Advisory Group 
to facilitate conversations and gain feedback on current initiatives. While the ESIM event 
focused on the needs of children, youth, and families system, most of the youth who were 
asked to participate expressed not feeling comfortable doing so. Therefore, youth focus groups 
were convened by Future Focused Education, El Puente, and NMCAN to provide the youth 
perspective regarding BH care.  Finally, all stakeholder meetings, were public and had a 
designated time devoted to public comment to facilitate feedback from non-voting members.  

 
 
 
 
8 
 
Outreach meetings have been convened with the Pueblo of Isleta, To’Hajiilee Navajo Chapter, 
and the Pueblo of Sandia to discuss the opportunities associated with BHRIA Regional Planning 
to ascertain the respective BH needs of these Indigenous communities.  
Following the submission of Region 2’s Plan, the Regional Stakeholder Committee will shift to a 
monthly meeting for the first six months of implementation. The need for subsequent meetings 
will be reassessed regarding the frequency of meetings moving forward. Additionally, Sandia 
and Isleta Pueblos will continue to be engaged through regular communications regarding 
regional planning. Each will be invited and welcomed to join the Stakeholder Committee 
Meetings at their discretion. As mentioned previously, the BernCo Website includes a BHRIA 
section dedicated to transparent community communication regarding regional planning and 
implementation. Stakeholder Committee meetings will remain public.  
Feedback loops are essential for program evaluation because they enable continuous quality 
improvement allowing BernCo to gather real-time data, identify patterns, and adjust strategies 
to improve effectiveness. This process will promote agility by facilitating quick responses to 
changing conditions, reducing risks, and boosting stakeholder engagement. By generating 
feedback loops, programs will be permitted to evolve by iterating design and delivery, based on 
direct input, ensuring maximum efficiency and impact.  By providing real-time data, 
organizations will be helped to quickly identify what is not working and adapt to changing 
environments, which is critical for staying relevant and effective.  Data-informed decision-
making will replace guesswork with evidence, allowing for informed, actionable, and objective 
improvements rather than relying on assumptions.  Where feedback is collected, acted upon, 
and reported back, value will be demonstrated, which can increase satisfaction and trust. These 
feedback mechanisms will act as a reality check, enabling BernCo to spot mistakes, avoid costly 
failures, and fix issues early before they escalate.  
BernCo will ensure that input collected from surveys, interviews, or debriefs is analyzed and 
subsequently leads to action, which is then communicated back to the service providers. This 
process will use both positive (reinforcing success) and negative (correcting failures) feedback in 
regular, iterative cycles, rather than only at the end of a given project implementation.  BernCo 
will also encourage an open and honest environment where feedback is seen as an opportunity 
for growth, rather than a personal or organizational critique. By implementing this type of 
evaluative process, organizations can achieve better outcomes.  
Regional Planning Structure: 1) Describe the governance and coordination structure used to 
guide development, implementation, and oversight of the regional plan. 2) Describe roles,  
 

 
 
 
 
9 
 
coordination mechanisms, and processes for collaboration, accountability, and ongoing review 
and updating of the regional plan.  
BernCo is responsible for all coordination, and oversight of implementation related to BHRIA 
projects. Since the inception of this legislation and BernCo’s identification as the Accountable 
Entity, every effort has been made to provide transparency to the community and to BH 
stakeholders. The potential utilization of HCA’s ASO will allow seamless delivery of real-time 
information to all stakeholders with a monthly status report that will be available on the BernCo 
Behavioral Health Authority Division web portal. If another distribution mechanism is chosen, 
BernCo will utilize its established Office of Data Collection, Analysis, and Reporting within the 
Behavioral Health Authority Division, to evaluate and report on key performance indicators 
(KPI), as it does for all funded BH services.  
BernCo has elected to utilize BHAB to guide the implementation of the Regional Plan as it will fit 
within its current advisory role, relative to BernCo’s BH Ordinance, its various strategic plans 
and their respective implementation. This body meets monthly and its Chair and Vice-Chair 
have been active members of the larger Stakeholder Committee and therefore they have been 
involved in Regional Plan development and planning since inception. The Stakeholder 
Committee is responsible for establishing a remediation process for BHRIA implementation with 
a success first approach. This is discussed more robustly in the Implementation Section of this 
Regional Plan.  
Priority Areas: 1) Describe priority areas and how it responds to regional needs and gaps 
identified through the regional needs assessment. 2) Identify the services and intended 
outcomes associated with each priority area. 3) Indicate whether proposed activities represent 
new services, expanded services, or enhancements to existing services, and describe how the 
plan build on current efforts where applicable.  
Region 2 has identified five priority areas: policy, access, continuum of care, social drivers of 
health, and workforce development. These priority areas were identified from an analysis of the 
ESIM event inputs which focused on the service needs of children, youth, and families and an 
analysis of other Sequential Intercept Model mapping projects, GAP Analysis, and strategic 
plans that have been conducted over recent years relative to the needs of adults and other 
plans and reports. The priority areas were refined from ESIM outputs to provide clear, 
actionable categories aligned with system-level gaps. The priority areas and their descriptions 
are as follows:  
 
 

 
 
 
 
10
 
 Policy: Advocating for laws, regulations, funding strategies, and administrative actions to 
improve the accessibility, quality, equity, integration, data integrity, and capacity; to 
improve outcomes related to the BHRIA initiatives across Region 2.  
 Access: Assuring access to timely, culturally sensitive, trauma responsive, and 
appropriate care by reducing regulatory, systemic, and cultural barriers to the BH 
system.  
 Continuum of Care: Building a comprehensive and coordinated system of BH services 
and supports that follow a person over time aimed at seamless care transitions from 
prevention to treatment and long-term supports.  
 Social Drivers of Health: Addressing the root conditions, that can be the largest 
contributors to positive BH outcomes. Solutions to address these root causes are 
typically not covered by Medicaid and therefore require a different sustainability plan.  
 Workforce Development: Building and strengthening a sustainable BH workforce that is 
well trained, culturally responsive, and financially supported across the full continuum of 
care.  
Please see the Description of Services section below for information related to the identification 
of services associated with each priority area.  
Expected outcomes include measurable improvements in access, service capacity, care 
coordination, and system integration. While Region 2 has the pillars of a BH system 
infrastructure, and capacity the connections between these pillars require further 
reinforcement and development. A benchmark for BHRIA success will be the degree to which 
access, prevention, early intervention, crisis response, intensive community-based levels of 
care, and care coordination are further developed and implemented across the system.   
Region 2 is evaluating the potential of utilizing HCA’s ASO for provider service agreements to 
include appropriate scopes of work (SOW) that will be negotiated subsequent to an evaluation 
of submitted proposals. BernCo also has the option to utilize providers that are approved 
through its Multi-Award procurement process. Funding determinations will be made through a 
structured proposal review process aligned with the five priority areas, with emphasis on 
sustainability and system impact. In addition, IGAs will be utilized as appropriate. Further, it will 
be challenging to utilize BHRIA funding for projects with recurring costs. For this reason, funding 
may need to be used largely for start-up costs, capital projects, and capacity-building. However, 
all proposals will be reviewed for relevance under the five priority areas and decisions will be 
made accordingly on how to make the most of the funding available, while working towards the 
overall sustainability of the system.

RISK & MITIGATION STRATEGY 
Applicants must identify potential risks or challenges that could affect successful implementation 
of the regional plan and describe strategies to mitigate those risks. This section should 
demonstrate awareness of barriers and proactive planning to minimize disruption. At a 
minimum, this section must address the following:  
Risk Identification: Identify key risks or challenges that could affect the regional plan, including 
barriers to successful implementation, service delivery, staffing, infrastructure, partnerships, 
funding, or system coordination, and describe their nature and potential impact.  
Some of the largest risk factors to a successful implementation and overall sustainability comes 
from the federal level decisions made around Medicaid, housing, and grant applications. To 
date, Public Law 119-21, otherwise known as The Big Beautiful Bill Act, has already begun 
shifting Medicaid work requirements that may make many ineligible. Further, federal policy has 
shifted away from the housing first model decreasing funding opportunities for those aligned 
programs. The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration has had funding cut 
in half. SAMHSA grants covered a large portion of mental health and substance abuse programs 
that may not be Medicaid eligible or who were serving populations without Medicaid or other 
health insurance. Finally, with the current federal administration taking a strong stance against 
diversity and equity, many grant proposals are being turned down based on population served 
or intended outcomes for minority populations including women and gender health. 
At the state level, there is a very real concern that the oil and gas industry is taking a downturn 
and the amount of money the state has been accustomed to working with, will dwindle making  

 
 
 
 
46
 
funding decisions that much more difficult. This development may be mitigated by the rising 
price of oil due to the Iranian conflict. Traditionally, mental health and substance abuse 
programs have been the first to receive cuts when states are faced with these financial 
decisions.   
These external factors present material risk to system sustainability, particularly for underserved 
populations, and require active mitigation strategies.  
Smaller, but equally important risks include the realities associated with project 
implementation, difficulties with proposal submission, over estimation of capacity, and difficulty 
finding sustainable and stable funding sources.    
Mitigation Strategies: Describe specific mitigation strategies for each identified risk, explain how 
they will reduce risk, maintain service fidelity, and support continuity of implementation, and 
identify responsible parties where applicable. 
BernCo is currently a Medicaid eligible provider. This is a huge step towards “freeing up” funding 
that has been previously earmarked for these programs that can bill Medicaid services. These 
additional dollars, expected to begin in FY28, can then be routed to support the non-Medicaid 
billable services programs inevitably provide.  
Further, BernCo has a BH Gross Receipt Tax (GRT) which also allows for flexibility for non-billable 
services to Medicaid or other payers.  
Behavioral Health Services Division (BHSD) under the Health Care Authority (HCA) has 
traditionally funded efforts in line with housing, forensic evaluation services, and other non-
Medicaid services. It is the hope that these programs continue to receive funding and continue 
to expand and develop over time. Similarly, treatment guardians are the backbone for safe 
community transitions for those with severe mental illness and are housed under the state 
Office of Guardianship and should continue to be funded and expanded to meet the needs of 
communities across the state. Meaning, state level offices should continue to support and 
expand statewide services.    
BernCo may be in a unique position in terms of the Behavioral Health Authority Ordinance to 
engage in capacity building, infrastructure, and technical support to reinforce the development, 
enhancement, and expansion of the BH continuum of care. This ordinance is in direct alignment 
with all BHRIA initiatives and Region 2 will work in tandem to develop and encourage successful
